story: Ordinary growth. Usage rises 8-12% across a few services, rates flat. Nothing here deserves a decision.
Container workload genuinely grew: Fargate vCPU-hours up 70% at an unchanged rate. The right question is what was deployed, and whether the traffic justifies it.
A one-year Compute Savings Plan expired. EC2 instance-hours are flat; the effective rate steps from the covered price back to on-demand. Nobody deployed anything.
expected_sentence: this is a rate change, not more usage

story: A promotional credit stopped applying. Usage is unchanged everywhere; the whole bill steps up because the offsetting credit line disappears.
expected_sentence: this is a rate change, not more usage

story: Egress volume quadrupled at an unchanged per-GB rate, and CloudFront moved with it. Compute is flat, so this is a traffic or payload change, not a deployment.
NAT gateway processed-GB up fivefold while EC2 compute-hours are flat: the signature of traffic routed through NAT that should not be, not of a bigger workload.
A container platform arrives in the last month with no history at all.
Inference demand grew: GPU instance-hours up 85% at the on-demand rate. Pairs with 09, where the hours are flat and only the rate moves.
The same GPU hours as last month, but spot capacity was interrupted and the fleet fell back to on-demand. Hours flat, effective rate up 2.8x.
expected_sentence: this is a rate change, not more usage

story: Grouped by the team tag. Untagged spend is already half the bill and grows faster than anything tagged, so most of the increase cannot be attributed to anyone.
Exported on the 18th, so the last month is 18 days of 31. A correct report refuses to compare it and says why.
Someone deleted old data and set a lifecycle policy: S3 GB-months down 34% at an unchanged rate. A report that only ever finds increases never gets tested on this.
A second account in eu-west-1 appears for an EU launch. Existing accounts are flat, so the whole increase sits in the new one.
Opened in Excel and saved again: byte-order mark, CRLF line endings, a title row above the header, and a total row someone edited so it no longer reconciles.
A European console export: semicolon delimiter, decimal comma, euro marker.
Half of a pair. A Cost Explorer export carries one metric, so this cost export has no quantities: on its own it cannot say whether usage or price moved.
expected_sentence: this is a rate change, not more usage

story: The other half: the same view re-exported with the Usage quantity metric. Together with 16a it shows hours flat while cost rose. Alone it is quantities with no currency, which a reader could mistake for money.
expected_sentence: this is a rate change, not more usage
